claims.source: Two modules contain left–right groups of parapodial and oblique muscles in the second and third segments, connected at the midline through the basal lamina and the median ventral longitudinal muscle (axochord or MUSax) (Lauri et al., 2014; Purschke and Müller, 2006).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes modules and cites studies on the axochord.

claims.claim: The other modules include parapodial muscles and chaetal sac cells, in the segmental parapodia.
claims.source: The other modules include parapodial muscles and chaetal sac cells, in the segmental parapodia.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the composition of additional modules.

claims.claim: Each module contains muscles and epidermal cells, and various other cell types.
claims.source: Each module contains muscles and epidermal cells, and various other cell types (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the cellular composition of modules.

claims.claim: The desmosomal graph stands out as a highly modular and less compact graph with strong local connectivity compared to simulated networks and the synaptic connectome.
claims.source: While all graph types have a similar degree and weighted degree distribution (Figure 4A, B), the desmosomal graph stands out as a highly modular and less compact graph with strong local connectivity. This conclusion is supported by several graph measures.
claims.evidence: The Results section compares the desmosomal graph to other graph types using multiple metrics.

claims.claim: The modularity scores of the subsampled desmosomal graphs are higher than for any other graph types, including the synaptic connectome.
claims.source: The modularity scores of the subsampled desmosomal graphs are higher than for any other graph types, including the synaptic connectome (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The Results section presents a specific graph metric comparison.

claims.claim: The desmosomal subgraphs have the largest graph diameter and the mean of the distances between vertices, both measures of graph compactness (Doyle and Graver, 1977).
claims.source: The desmosomal subgraphs have the largest graph diameter (the length of the longest graph geodesic between any two vertices) and the mean of the distances between vertices (Figure 4D, E), both measures of graph compactness (Doyle and Graver, 1977).
claims.evidence: The Results section presents graph metrics and cites a reference for their interpretation.

claims.claim: The desmosomal and synaptic connectome graphs have the highest transitivity values (clustering coefficient), which measures the probability that nodes connected to the same node are also directly connected to each other.
claims.source: The desmosomal and synaptic connectome graphs have the highest transitivity values (clustering coefficient), which measures the probability that nodes connected to the same node are also directly connected to each other (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: The Results section presents another graph metric comparison.

claims.claim: The number of 3-cliques (three fully connected nodes) ranks the synaptic graph as first followed by the desmosomal graph.
claims.source: A similar measure, the number of 3-cliques (three fully connected nodes) also ranks the synaptic graph as first followed by the desmosomal graph (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: The Results section presents another graph metric comparison.

claims.claim: The assortativity coefficient is lowest for the desmosomal graph, indicating more connections between nodes of different degree.
claims.source: The assortativity coefficient (between −1 and 1), a measure of the extent to which nodes of similar degree are connected (1 for the preferential-attachment graphs) is lowest for the desmosomal graph, indicating more connections between nodes of different degree (Figure 4H).
claims.evidence: The Results section presents and interprets the assortativity coefficient.

claims.claim: The desmosomal graph is characterized by high modularity, large diameter, large average distance, and high level of local connectivity (cliques).
claims.source: Overall, the desmosomal graph stands out as a highly modular graph with a large diameter, large average distance, and high level of local connectivity (cliques).
claims.evidence: The Results section summarizes the key characteristics of the desmosomal graph.

claims.claim: These properties set the desmosomal graph apart from different types of random graphs and the synaptic connectome.
claims.source: These properties set the desmosomal graph apart from different types of random graphs and the synaptic connectome.
claims.evidence: The Results section contrasts the desmosomal graph with other graph types.

claims.claim: The special organization of the desmosomal connectome is attributed to all cells only connecting to cells in their immediate neighbourhood forming local cliques, and without long-range connections.
claims.source: We attribute these characteristics to the special organisation of the desmosomal connectome, with all cells only connecting to cells in their immediate neighbourhood forming local cliques, and without long-range connections (e.g. between the left and right body sides).
claims.evidence: The Results section provides an interpretation for the observed graph properties.

claims.claim: In the force-field layout, nodes are segregated by body side and body segment.
claims.source: To analyse how closely the force-field-based layout of the desmosomal connectome reflects anatomy, we coloured the nodes in the graph based on body regions (Figure 5). In the force-field layout, nodes are segregated by body side and body segment.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the spatial organization of nodes in the force-field layout.

claims.claim: The observation that node positions in the force-field layout of the graph recapitulate the anatomical positions of the nodes reflects the local connectedness (neighbours only) of the desmosomal connectome.
claims.source: The observation that node positions in the force-field layout of the graph recapitulate the anatomical positions of the nodes reflects the local connectedness (neighbours only) of the desmosomal connectome.
claims.evidence: The Results section interprets the correspondence between graph layout and anatomy.

claims.claim: This is different from the synaptic connectome where long-range neurite projections can link neurons at two different ends of the body (Verasztó et al., 2020).
claims.source: This is different from the synaptic connectome where long-range neurite projections can link neurons at two different ends of the body (Verasztó et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The Results section contrasts the desmosomal connectome with the synaptic connectome and cites a previous study.

claims.claim: In the segmented larva, each parapodium has a dorsal and a ventral lobe (notopodium and neuropodium).
claims.source: In the segmented larva, each parapodium has a dorsal and a ventral lobe (notopodium and neuropodium).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the anatomy of the parapodium.

claims.claim: Each lobe is supported by an internal chitinous rod called acicula that is ensheathed by acicular follicle cells.
claims.source: Each lobe is supported by an internal chitinous rod called acicula (Hausen, 2005) that is ensheathed by acicular follicle cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, C).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the structure of the acicula and cites a previous study.

claims.claim: Each parapodial lobe contains a chaetal sac consisting of bristle-producing chaetoblasts, chaetal follicle cells, epidermal cells, and bristle mechanosensory neurons (chaeMech) (Verasztó et al., 2020).
claims.source: Each parapodial lobe also contains a chaetal sac consisting of bristle-producing chaetoblasts, chaetal follicle cells, epidermal cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, C), and bristle mechanosensory neurons (chaeMech) (Verasztó et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the composition of the chaetal sac and cites a previous study.

claims.claim: The chaetal follicle cells ensheathing the chaetae have four types arranged in a proximo-distal pattern.
claims.source: The chaetal follicle cells ensheathing the chaetae have four types arranged in a proximo-distal pattern (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the organization of chaetal follicle cells.

claims.claim: The aciculoblasts, chaetoblasts, and the various follicle cells serve as anchor points for several major parapodial muscle groups.
claims.source: The aciculoblasts, chaetoblasts, and the various follicle cells serve as anchor points for several major parapodial muscle groups (Figure 6E–I, Figure 1E, Video 4).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the functional role of follicle cells in muscle attachment.

claims.claim: The aciculae and associated structures in the parapodial complex represent highly connected components in the desmosomal connectome.
claims.source: The aciculae and associated structures in the parapodial complex represent highly connected components in the desmosomal connectome (Figure 6E–G).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the connectivity of aciculae in the network.

claims.claim: The cells with the largest mean degree and weighted degree belong to the parapodial complex.
claims.source: The cells with the largest mean degree and weighted degree belong to the parapodial complex.
claims.evidence: The Results section identifies the most highly connected cells in the network.

claims.claim: 16 muscle types have connections to the aciculae or to acicular follicle cells.
claims.source: We identified 16 muscle types with connections to the aciculae or to acicular follicle cells (Figure 6F, G; Figure 6—figure supplement 2; Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: The Results section quantifies the number of muscle types connected to aciculae.

claims.claim: These include acicular muscles (MUSac), some chaetal muscles (MUSchae) that link the aciculae to the chaetae and oblique muscles (MUSob) that link the aciculae to the dorsal longitudinal muscles (MUSlongD).
claims.source: These include acicular muscles (MUSac), some chaetal muscles (MUSchae) that link the aciculae to the chaetae and oblique muscles (MUSob) that link the aciculae to the dorsal longitudinal muscles (MUSlongD).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the types of muscles connected to aciculae.

claims.claim: Several acicular muscles attach on one end to the proximal base of the aciculae and on the other end to the paratrochs and epidermal cells.
claims.source: Several acicular muscles attach on one end to the proximal base of the aciculae and on the other end to the paratrochs and epidermal cells.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the attachment sites of acicular muscles.

claims.claim: Oblique muscles attach to the basal lamina, epidermal, and midline cells at their proximal end, run along the anterior edge of parapodia and attach to epidermal and chaetal follicle cells at their distal tips.
claims.source: Oblique muscles attach to the basal lamina, epidermal, and midline cells at their proximal end, run along the anterior edge of parapodia and attach to epidermal and chaetal follicle cells at their distal tips (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, Videos 2 and 4).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the attachment sites and trajectory of oblique muscles.

claims.claim: Both acicular and oblique muscle groups are involved in moving the entire parapodium.
claims.source: Both of these muscle groups are involved in moving the entire parapodium.
claims.evidence: The Results section infers the functional role of these muscle groups.

claims.claim: Acicular muscles move the proximal tips of the aciculae, while oblique muscles move the parapodium by moving the tissue around the chaetae and the aciculae.
claims.source: Acicular muscles move the proximal tips of the aciculae, while oblique muscles move the parapodium by moving the tissue around the chaetae and the aciculae.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the distinct mechanisms by which different muscle groups move the parapodium.

claims.claim: All acicular movements also correspond to parapodial movements.
claims.source: All acicular movements also correspond to parapodial movements.
claims.evidence: The Results section states the relationship between acicular and parapodial movements.

claims.claim: Chaetae are embedded in the parapodium and therefore move with it, but the chaetal sac muscles can also independently retract the chaetae into the parapodium or protract them and make them fan out.
claims.source: Chaetae are embedded in the parapodium and therefore move with it, but the chaetal sac muscles can also independently retract the chaetae into the parapodium or protract them and make them fan out.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the movements of chaetae and their relationship to parapodial movements.

claims.claim: The notopodial and neuropodical aciculae have distinct muscle partners indicating that these structures could move independent of each other.
claims.source: The notopodial and neuropodical aciculae have distinct muscle partners indicating that these structures could move independent of each other.
claims.evidence: The Results section infers functional independence from distinct connectivity patterns.

claims.claim: Two muscles (MUSac-i and MUSac-neuDx) link the noto- and neuropodial aciculae within the same parapodium to each other, suggesting force coupling between the two aciculae.
claims.source: Two muscles (MUSac-i and MUSac-neuDx) link the noto- and neuropodial aciculae within the same parapodium to each other, suggesting force coupling between the two aciculae (Figure 6E, G).
claims.evidence: The Results section identifies muscles that couple the two aciculae and infers their functional role.

claims.claim: Analysis of each muscle group for their desmosomal partners and spatial orientation revealed several possible acicular movements termed extension, flexion, pivoting, abduction, chaetal retraction, and jostling.
claims.source: We analysed each muscle group for their desmosomal partners and spatial orientation and inferred the possible movements of the aciculae upon their contraction. This revealed several possible acicular movements which we termed extension, flexion, pivoting, abduction, chaetal retraction, and jostling (Figure 6—figure supplement 4, Video 2, Video 4).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the inference of acicular movements from anatomical data.

claims.claim: Some muscles connect to epidermal cells in the parapodium and through moving these epidermal cells can indirectly also move the aciculae (i.e. 'pulled by the skin'; e.g. MUSobP-neuV).
claims.source: In addition, some muscles connect to epidermal cells in the parapodium and through moving these epidermal cells can indirectly also move the aciculae (i.e. 'pulled by the skin'; e.g. MUSobP-neuV) (Video 4).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes an indirect mechanism of acicular movement.

claims.claim: The movement of the parapodia during crawling requires connections to the axochord muscle (MUSax) at the midline.
claims.source: The movement of the parapodia during crawling also requires connections to the axochord muscle (MUSax) at the midline.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the role of the axochord in parapodial movement.

claims.claim: Animals with an ablated axochord show impaired crawling indicating a structural role for this muscle (Lauri et al., 2014).
claims.source: Animals with an ablated axochord show impared crawling indicating a structural role for this muscle (Lauri et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The Results section cites an experimental study demonstrating the functional importance of the axochord.

claims.claim: A high density of hemidesmosomes between the axochord and the extracellular matrix dorsal to the neuronal midline agrees with a structural role for the axochord.
claims.source: A high density of hemidesmosomes between the axochord and the extracellular matrix dorsal to the neuronal midline agrees with this (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B, D).
claims.evidence: The Results section relates anatomical observations to functional inferences.

claims.claim: The extracellular matrix on the midline serves as an attachment site for the proximal ends of anterior and posterior oblique muscles and the radial-glia-like midline cells that are rich in tonofibrils.
claims.source: The extracellular matrix on the midline also serves as an attachment site for the proximal ends of anterior and posterior oblique muscles and the radial-glia-like midline cells that are rich in tonofibrils.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the attachment sites on the midline extracellular matrix.

claims.claim: The desmosomal connectome suggests that each acicula can have complex and extensive movements and the two aciculae can move independently of each other, with some coupling.
claims.source: The desmosomal connectome suggests that each acicula can have complex and extensive movements and the two aciculae can move independently of each other, with some coupling (e.g. through the inter-acicular muscles).
claims.evidence: The Results section summarizes inferences about acicular movements from the connectome data.

claims.claim: The organization of the musculature in 3- and 4-day-old three-segmented larvae is very similar.
claims.source: The organisation of the musculature in 3- and 4-day-old three-segmented larvae is very similar (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), therefore we could relate movements in the more active 4-day-old larvae to the EM data.
claims.evidence: The Results section justifies the use of 4-day-old larvae for movement analysis by comparing their musculature to 3-day-old larvae.

claims.claim: DeepLabCut was used to train a deep residual neural network to track and label 26 body parts of the larvae.
claims.source: We used the toolbox DeepLabCut (Mathis et al., 2018) to train a deep residual neural network using sample video frames to learn, track, and label 26 body parts of the larvae.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the method used for tracking body parts.

claims.claim: The notopodial and neuropodial aciculae within one parapodium exhibit differences in movement velocity and angles relative to one another resulting in a range of angles and positions over time.
claims.source: We found that the notopodial and neuropodial aciculae within one parapodium exhibit differences in movement velocity and angles relative to one another resulting in a range of angles and positions over time (Figure 7, Video 5).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the observed movements of aciculae from video tracking.

claims.claim: During the crawl cycles, the aciculae first draw inwards and forwards, diagonally towards the head, then they tilt in a posterior direction, the proximal tip of the neuropodial acicula travelling slightly faster to open up the pair, creating the larger (40–50°) inter-acicular angle.
claims.source: During the crawl cycles, the aciculae first draw inwards and forwards, diagonally towards the head, then they tilt in a posterior direction, the proximal tip of the neuropodial acicula travelling slightly faster to open up the pair, creating the larger (40–50°) inter-acicular angle (Figure 7E–G).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the sequence of acicular movements during crawling.

claims.claim: The acicular cycle is completed by a 'piston' movement whereby the now parallel aciculae are pushed outwards, then the proximal tips tilt rostrally again, to move the chaetae back against the trunk, propelling the animal forward on that side.
claims.source: This is followed by a 'piston' movement whereby the now parallel aciculae are pushed outwards, then the proximal tips tilt rostrally again, to move the chaetae back against the trunk, propelling the animal forward on that side and completing that acicular cycle.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the completion of the acicular movement cycle.

claims.claim: The acicular pairs can have different relative positions with inter-acicular angles changing between −25° and 50° in one parapodial cycle.
claims.source: This analysis demonstrates that the acicular pairs can have different relative positions with inter-acicular angles changing between −25° and 50° in one parapodial cycle (Figure 7B, G).
claims.evidence: The Results section quantifies the range of inter-acicular angles during movement.

claims.claim: These relative changes occur in each segment during crawling, propagating from posterior to anterior through an undulatory gait cycle.
claims.source: These relative changes occur in each segment during crawling, propagating from posterior to anterior through an undulatory gait cycle (Figure 7A).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the spatial and temporal pattern of acicular movements during crawling.

claims.claim: The contraction of the posterior ventral neuropodial acicular muscle (MUSac-neuPV) pulls the proximal end of the acicula caudally, inducing an abduction.
claims.source: The contraction of the posterior ventral neuropodial acicular muscle (MUSac-neuPV) pulls the proximal end of the acicula caudally, inducing an abduction (Figure 7H; Figure 6—figure supplement 4E).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the movement induced by a specific muscle contraction observed in live imaging.

claims.claim: MUSac-neuPV muscles connect to the proximal end of the acicula via acicular follicle cells and anchor to the basal lamina, epidermal cells and ciliated cells (paratroch) at their other end.
claims.source: These muscles connect to the proximal end of the acicula via acicular follicle cells and anchor to the basal lamina, epidermal cells and ciliated cells (paratroch) at their other end (Figure 7K).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the desmosomal connectivity of MUSac-neuPV.

claims.claim: The contraction of the posterior ventral neuropodial muscles (MUSobP-neuV) induces an inward movement of the distal tip of the acicula ('flexion') leading to the alignment of the parapodia and chaetae with the longitudinal body axis.
claims.source: The contraction of the posterior ventral neuropodial muscles (MUSobP-neuV) induces an inward movement of the distal tip of the acicula ('flexion', Figure 6—figure supplement 4B) leading to the alignment of the parapodia and chaetae with the longitudinal body axis (Figure 7I).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the movement induced by MUSobP-neuV contraction.

claims.claim: MUSobP-neuV cells connect to the distal end of the aciculae via acicular follicle cells and also connect to epidermal cells in the neuropodium. At their other end, MUSobP-neuV cells are anchored to the basal lamina.
claims.source: These muscles connect to the distal end of the aciculae via acicular follicle cells and also connect to epidermal cells in the neuropodium. At their other end, MUSobP-neuV cells are anchored to the basal lamina (Figure 7L).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the desmosomal connectivity of MUSobP-neuV.

claims.claim: The MUSac-neuPV cells can contract simultaneously with the parapodial retractor muscles (MUSobA-re), inducing parapodial retraction and a tilt of the aciculae with their proximal tip moving rostrally.
claims.source: The MUSac-neuPV cells can contract simultaneously with the parapodial retractor muscles (MUSobA-re), inducing parapodial retraction and a tilt of the aciculae with their proximal tip moving rostrally (Figure 7J).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the coordinated contraction of two muscle types and the resulting movement.

claims.claim: The retractor muscles form desmosomes on chaeFC-EC (epidermal chaetal follicle) and epidermal cells at their distal end in the neuropodium and anchor to ventral midline cells and the basal lamina at their other end.
claims.source: The retractor muscles form desmosomes on chaeFC-EC (epidermal chaetal follicle) and epidermal cells at their distal end in the neuropodium and anchor to ventral midline cells and the basal lamina at their other end (Figure 7M).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the desmosomal connectivity of retractor muscles.

claims.claim: During a startle response or crawling cycles, many muscles contract rapidly (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018) and individual muscle contractions could not be spatially and temporally resolved.
claims.source: We could only observe these spontaneous individual muscle contractions in non-crawling larvae. During a startle response or crawling cycles, many muscles contract rapidly (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018) and we were not able to spatially and temporally resolve these to individual muscle groups.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the limitations of the imaging approach and cites a previous study.

claims.claim: The availability of full desmosomal and synaptic connectomes (Verasztó et al., 2020) for the same Platynereis larva allowed analysis of how individual motoneurons could influence muscles and associated tissues.
claims.source: The availability of full desmosomal and synaptic connectomes (Verasztó et al., 2020) for the same Platynereis larva allowed us to analyse how individual motoneurons could influence muscles and associated tissues.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the integration of synaptic and desmosomal data and cites the source of the synaptic connectome.

claims.claim: By combining desmosomal and synaptic connectomes we can infer the impact of motoneuron activation on tissue movements.
claims.source: Motoneuron activation is expected to induce postsynaptic muscle contraction, which will exert forces on the desmosomal partners of the muscle. By combining desmosomal and synaptic connectomes we can infer the impact of motoneuron activation on tissue movements (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the rationale for combining the two connectomes.

claims.claim: 11 motoneuron types that are well developed in the 3-day-old larva were analyzed (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018; Verasztó et al., 2020).
claims.source: We analysed 11 motoneuron types that are well developed in the 3-day-old larva (Bezares-Calderón et al., 2018; Verasztó et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The Results section specifies the motoneuron types analyzed and cites previous studies.

claims.claim: The 11 motoneuron types collectively provide broad innervation across the entire muscle network.
claims.source: These collectively provide broad innervation across the entire muscle network (Figure 8A).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the overall pattern of motoneuron innervation.

claims.claim: All motoneurons have multiple muscle targets and most muscles receive synapses from more than one motoneuron.
claims.source: All motoneurons have multiple muscle targets and most muscles receive synapses from more than one motoneuron.
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the convergence and divergence of motoneuron-muscle connections.

claims.claim: When the most highly connected muscle in the parapodial complex (MUSchae-notAac) contracts, it is expected to transmit the forces of the contraction through desmosomes to up to nine distinct non-muscle cell types.
claims.source: For example, when the most highly connected muscle in the parapodial complex (MUSchae-notAac) contracts, it is expected to transmit the forces of the contraction through desmosomes to up to nine distinct non-muscle cell types (Figure 9).
claims.evidence: The Results section provides an example of the extent of tissue influenced by a single muscle contraction.

claims.claim: There are eight motoneuron cell types that innervate the parapodial complex (MNcrab, MNbiramous, MNwave, MNspider-ant, MNspider-post, MNhose, MNchae, and MNring).
claims.source: There are eight motoneuron cell types that innervate the parapodial complex (MNcrab, MNbiramous, MNwave, MNspider-ant, MNspider-post, MNhose, MNchae, and MNring).
claims.evidence: The Results section lists the motoneuron types that innervate the parapodial complex.

claims.claim: Each of the eight motoneuron types innervating the parapodial complex innervates a unique combination of muscle targets – not a single muscle type.
claims.source: Each of these innervates a unique combination of muscle targets – not a single muscle type (Figure 10).
claims.evidence: The Results section describes the specificity of motoneuron innervation patterns.

claims.claim: The unique innervation patterns suggest the concerted activity of anatomically distinct muscle types during the parapodial crawl cycle and other appendage movements.
claims.source: This suggests the concerted activity of anatomically distinct muscle types during the parapodial crawl cycle and other appendage movements.
claims.evidence: The Results section infers functional coordination from innervation patterns.

claims.claim: The reconstructions revealed the high diversity of muscle cell types in the larva.
claims.source: Here, we reconstructed the somatic musculature and attached tissues in the nereid larva and showed how adhesion networks can be analysed for an entire body. We call this approach desmosomal connectomics, where the desmosomal connectome comprises all cells and extracellular structures (basal lamina, aciculae, and chaeta) and their desmosomal connections. Our reconstructions revealed the high diversity of muscle cell types in the larva.
claims.evidence: The Discussion summarizes a key finding of the study.

claims.claim: The complexity of the nereid musculature contrasts to the relatively simple muscle architecture in the nematode C. elegans and the tadpole larva of the tunicate Ciona intestinalis.
claims.source: The complexity of the nereid musculature contrasts to the relatively simple muscle architecture in the nematode C. elegans and the tadpole larva of the tunicate Ciona intestinalis.
claims.evidence: The Discussion compares the complexity of the nereid musculature to other organisms.

claims.claim: The C. elegans hermaphrodite has 95 body wall muscles all with a similar rhomboid shape (Gieseler et al., 2017).
claims.source: The C. elegans hermaphrodite has 95 body wall muscles all with a similar rhomboid shape (Gieseler et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a study on C. elegans muscle anatomy for comparison.

claims.claim: In the C. intestinalis larva, there are 36 muscle cells of 10 types (Nakamura et al., 2012).
claims.source: In the C. intestinalis larva, there are 36 muscle cells of 10 types (Nakamura et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites a study on Ciona muscle anatomy for comparison.

claims.claim: In contrast, the 3-day-old nereid larva has 853 muscle cells belonging to 53 types.
claims.source: In contrast, the 3-day-old nereid larva has 853 muscle cells belonging to 53 types.
claims.evidence: The Discussion contrasts the nereid larva with C. elegans and Ciona.

claims.claim: A large number of muscles engage in the movement of the parapodial muscle complex.
claims.source: A large number of muscles engage in the movement of the parapodial muscle complex.
claims.evidence: The Discussion summarizes a key finding about the parapodial complex.

claims.claim: The diversity of nereid somatic muscles is due to the presence of an endoskeleton.
claims.source: This suggests that the diversity of nereid somatic muscles is due to the presence of an endoskeleton.
claims.evidence: The Discussion proposes an explanation for muscle diversity.

claims.claim: Polychaete annelids are the only animals outside the tetrapods that have trunk appendages rigidified by an endoskeleton.
claims.source: Polychaete annelids are the only animals outside the tetrapods that have trunk appendages rigidified by an endoskeleton.
claims.evidence: The Discussion states a unique anatomical feature of polychaetes.

claims.claim: Aciculae probably evolved in the stem group of errant annelids around the Early Ordovician (Parry et al., 2019; Vinther et al., 2008) indicating the deep ancestry of these structures, predating tetrapod limbs.
claims.source: Aciculae probably evolved in the stem group of errant annelids around the Early Ordovician (Parry et al., 2019; Vinther et al., 2008) indicating the deep ancestry of these structures, predating tetrapod limbs.
claims.evidence: The Discussion cites studies on the evolutionary origin of aciculae.

claims.claim: In contrast to tetrapod limb bones, the aciculae are independent skeletal elements without joints.
claims.source: In contrast to tetrapod limb bones, the aciculae are independent skeletal elements without joints.
claims.evidence: The Discussion contrasts aciculae with tetrapod limb bones.

claims.claim: The function of aciculae is similar to tetrapod limb bones in that they provide attachment sites for limb muscles and rigidity in the appendages during movement.
claims.source: Their function is nevertheless similar in that they provide attachment sites for limb muscles and rigidity in the appendages during movement.
claims.evidence: The Discussion compares the functional role of aciculae to tetrapod limb bones.

claims.claim: In each parapodium, the two aciculae are moved by unique and shared sets of muscles and change their relative angle within a crawling cycle.
claims.source: In each parapodium, the two aciculae are moved by unique and shared sets of muscles and change their relative angle within a crawling cycle.
claims.evidence: The Discussion summarizes findings on acicular movements.

claims.claim: The stereotypy of the desmosomal connections across segments and body sides suggests that the desmosomal connectome develops through a precisely specified connectivity code between cell types.
claims.source: The stereotypy of the desmosomal connections across segments and body sides suggests that – analogous to the synaptic connectome – the desmosomal connectome develops through a precisely specified connectivity code between cell types.
claims.evidence: The Discussion infers developmental mechanisms from the observed stereotypy.

claims.claim: Some desmosomal connections have a clear functional relevance, as the attachment of muscles to movable chitin structures.
claims.source: Some of these connections have a clear functional relevance, as the attachment of muscles to movable chitin structures.
claims.evidence: The Discussion interprets the functional significance of some desmosomal connections.

claims.claim: Connections to locomotor ciliary cells may be due to proximity and the need for muscles to attach to something, alternatively, may mediate hitherto unexplored mechanistic interactions between muscular and ciliary locomotion or represent signalling connections (Green and Gaudry, 2000).
claims.source: Others are more intriguing, such as the connections to locomotor ciliary cells. These may be due to proximity and the need for muscles to attach to something, alternatively, may mediate hitherto unexplored mechanistic interactions between muscular and ciliary locomotion or represent signalling connections (Green and Gaudry, 2000).
claims.evidence: The Discussion speculates on the functional significance of connections to ciliary cells and cites a relevant study.

claims.claim: The whole-body desmosomal connectome in combination with the synaptic connectome from the same volume (Verasztó et al., 2020) provide the foundation for understanding locomotor control in the nereid larva.
claims.source: The whole-body desmosomal connectome described here in combination with the synaptic connectome from the same volume (Verasztó et al., 2020) provide the foundation for understanding locomotor control in the nereid larva.
claims.evidence: The Discussion states the significance of the combined connectomes and cites the synaptic connectome study.

claims.claim: In a crawling larva, the contraction of a large number of muscles is recruited in a precise temporal order in each limb to execute a full appendage cycle.
claims.source: In a crawling larva, the contraction of a large number of muscles is recruited in a precise temporal order in each limb to execute a full appendage cycle.
claims.evidence: The Discussion describes the coordination of muscle contractions during crawling.

claims.claim: The limb movements are organised into a gait sequence, starting from the posterior-most segment.
claims.source: The limb movements are organised into a gait sequence, starting from the posterior-most segment (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: The Discussion describes the spatial organization of the gait sequence.

claims.claim: The imaging of spontaneous muscle twitches, prediction of unit acicular movements and analysis of motoneuron innervation are the first steps towards understanding parapodial movements and their neuronal control.
claims.source: Our imaging of spontaneous muscle twitches (Figure 8), prediction of unit acicular movements (Figure 6—figure supplement 4) and analysis of motoneuron innervation (Figure 9) are the first steps towards understanding parapodial movements and their neuronal control.
claims.evidence: The Discussion summarizes the contributions of the study towards understanding locomotor control.

claims.claim: The availability of a laboratory culture, whole-body connectome and a growing repertoire of genetic tools make the nereid larva a promising experimental system for the in-depth analysis of locomotor control.
claims.source: The availability of a laboratory culture, whole-body connectome and a growing repertoire of genetic tools make the nereid larva a promising experimental system for the in-depth analysis of locomotor control.
claims.evidence: The Discussion argues for the utility of the nereid larva as a model system.

claims.claim: In Platynereis, as well as in other animals, understanding and accurately modelling locomotion will require analysing nervous activity and synaptic contacts, as well as comprehensive maps of the adhesive networks of muscle systems.
claims.source: We argue that in Platynereis, as well as in other animals, understanding and accurately modelling locomotion will not only require analysing nervous activity and synaptic contacts, but also comprehensive maps of the adhesive networks of muscle systems.
claims.evidence: The Discussion argues for the importance of studying both synaptic and desmosomal networks.

results.result: The authors reconstructed 853 muscle cells and all other cells in a 3-day-old Platynereis larva from whole-body serial TEM data by skeletonization, marking soma positions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C47-C50 collectively describe the reconstruction methodology and quantify the number of muscle cells identified (853 mononucleated muscle cells). The methodology is clearly described (skeletonization, soma marking) and the data source is cited (Randel et al., 2015). The figures referenced provide visual evidence of the reconstructions.

results.result: The desmosomal connectome comprises over 2000 cells (2807 nodes total, 2095 with soma) connected by 6961 edges, with muscles adhering to diverse cell types including epithelial, glial, ciliated, bristle-producing cells, and basal lamina. Only 2.4% of desmosomes connect muscle-to-muscle, suggesting desmosomes do not mediate lateral force transmission between muscles of the same bundle.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C3 and C66-C72 provide comprehensive quantitative data on the desmosomal connectome composition and connectivity patterns. The low proportion of muscle-to-muscle connections (C68) supports the inference about lack of lateral force transmission (C69). The data are internally consistent and well-documented with specific percentages and counts.

results.result: The 853 muscle cells were classified into 8 main groups and 53 distinct types based on position, shape, motoneuron inputs, and desmosomal partners, with stereotyped segmental repetition and left-right symmetry suggesting specification by unique developmental programs.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 describe a comprehensive classification scheme with clear criteria (position, shape, connectivity, innervation). The stereotypy observed (C57) and the comparison to Drosophila (C58) provide reasonable support for the developmental inference, though this remains an inference rather than direct experimental evidence.

results.result: The majority of muscle types (34/53 types, 502/853 cells) form the parapodial muscle complex, with segmental variation in the first segment and a cryptic segment 0 lacking parapodia.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C62 provide specific quantitative data on the distribution of muscle types across body segments. The segmental variation is documented with specific missing muscle types (C60), and the developmental fate of segment 1 parapodia is supported by citation (C61).

results.result: Aciculae (chitin rods forming an endoskeleton) are highly connected hubs in the desmosomal network, with 16 muscle types connecting to aciculae or acicular follicle cells, and this high connectivity correlates with many degrees of freedom in acicular movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6 and C96-C99 establish both the structural role of aciculae and their network properties. The high connectivity is quantified (16 muscle types, C98) and supported by network analysis (C96-C97). The correlation with movement degrees of freedom (C6) is supported by video microscopy data described later in the manuscript.

results.result: Leiden algorithm analysis revealed modular organization of the desmosomal connectome into anatomically distinct territories including four longitudinal muscle modules, head/segment-0 module, segmental parapodial modules, and modules connected at the midline through the axochord.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C78 describe the modularity analysis results with specific anatomical interpretations. The use of the Leiden algorithm is appropriate for community detection, and the correspondence between modules and anatomical territories is documented with figures. The biological interpretation is reasonable given the local connectivity patterns.

results.result: The desmosomal graph exhibits high modularity, large diameter, large average distance, high transitivity, and low assortativity compared to random graphs and the synaptic connectome, reflecting local-only connectivity without long-range connections.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C87 present comprehensive graph-theoretic analysis comparing the desmosomal connectome to 1000 simulated graphs of each type and the synaptic connectome. Multiple metrics consistently support the conclusion of high modularity and local connectivity. The interpretation (C87) logically follows from the quantitative results.

results.result: Force-field layout of the desmosomal connectome recapitulates anatomical positions, with nodes segregated by body side and segment, reflecting local-only connectivity unlike the synaptic connectome which has long-range connections.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 describe how graph layout reflects anatomy. The correspondence between force-field layout and anatomical position (C88-C89) is documented with figures, and the contrast with the synaptic connectome (C90) is appropriately cited. This provides independent validation of the local connectivity conclusion.

results.result: Each parapodial lobe contains an acicula ensheathed by acicular follicle cells and a chaetal sac with four types of chaetal follicle cells arranged proximo-distally, serving as anchor points for parapodial muscles.
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C95 describe the detailed anatomy of the parapodial complex with appropriate citations (C92-C93) and documentation of follicle cell types (C94). The functional role as muscle anchor points (C95) is supported by the desmosomal connectivity data presented.

results.result: Acicular and oblique muscles attach to aciculae and move the parapodium through distinct mechanisms, with notopodial and neuropodial aciculae having distinct muscle partners allowing independent movement with some coupling through inter-acicular muscles.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C109 describe the attachment patterns and inferred movements of different muscle groups. The anatomical connectivity is well-documented (C100-C101), and the functional inferences (C102-C109) are reasonable based on the attachment sites and muscle orientations. However, these remain inferences from anatomy rather than direct functional measurements.

results.result: The axochord muscle at the midline is required for crawling, as shown by ablation experiments, and has high density of hemidesmosomes to the extracellular matrix, which also serves as attachment for oblique muscles and midline cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C113 combine functional evidence from ablation experiments (C111, cited) with anatomical observations of hemidesmosome density (C112). The convergence of functional and structural data strongly supports the structural role of the axochord in parapodial movement.

results.result: Video tracking with DeepLabCut of 4-day-old larvae (similar musculature to 3-day-old) revealed that notopodial and neuropodial aciculae exhibit complex movements with inter-acicular angles changing between -25° and 50° during crawling cycles, propagating posterior to anterior.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C121 describe the video tracking methodology and quantitative results. The justification for using 4-day-old larvae is provided (C115), the tracking method is appropriate (C116), and the movement patterns are quantified with specific angle ranges (C120). The data directly validate predictions from the anatomical analysis.

results.result: Live calcium imaging of spontaneous muscle contractions revealed specific movements induced by individual muscle groups: MUSac-neuPV induces abduction, MUSobP-neuV induces flexion, and MUSobA-re induces parapodial retraction, with desmosomal connectivity patterns explaining the observed movements.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C127 link specific muscle contractions (observed via GCaMP6s) to specific movements and their desmosomal connectivity patterns. This provides direct functional validation of the anatomical predictions. The limitation that complex movements during crawling could not be resolved (C128) is appropriately acknowledged.

results.result: Integration of synaptic and desmosomal connectomes for 11 motoneuron types revealed that motoneurons have multiple muscle targets, most muscles receive input from multiple motoneurons, and muscle contraction can influence up to 9 distinct non-muscle cell types through desmosomal connections.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C129-C134 describe the integration of two connectome datasets to infer the extent of tissue influenced by motoneurons. The approach is sound and the data are from the same specimen. The example of MUSchae-notAac (C134) illustrates the broad tissue influence. This represents a novel analytical approach combining two types of connectivity data.

results.result: Eight motoneuron types innervate the parapodial complex, each innervating unique combinations of muscle types rather than single types, suggesting concerted activity of anatomically distinct muscles during parapodial movements.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C137 describe the innervation patterns of parapodial motoneurons. The observation that each motoneuron innervates multiple muscle types (C136) is well-documented, and the inference about concerted activity (C137) is reasonable, though it remains an inference rather than direct measurement of coordinated activity.

results.result: The Platynereis larva has 853 muscle cells of 53 types, far more complex than C. elegans (95 muscles) or Ciona (36 muscles of 10 types), with this diversity attributed to the presence of an endoskeleton (aciculae).
results.evaluation: Claims C138-C144 compare muscle complexity across species with appropriate citations (C140-C141). The quantitative comparison is clear and the inference that endoskeletal elements drive muscle diversity (C144) is reasonable, though this remains a hypothesis rather than experimentally tested causation.

results.result: Polychaete annelids are unique outside tetrapods in having trunk appendages with an endoskeleton (aciculae), which evolved in the Early Ordovician and function similarly to tetrapod limb bones by providing muscle attachment sites and rigidity, with the two aciculae per parapodium moved by unique and shared muscle sets.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C149 place the findings in evolutionary context with appropriate citations (C146). The functional comparison to tetrapod limbs (C148) is reasonable while noting structural differences (C147). The summary of acicular movements (C149) is supported by the data presented earlier.

results.result: The stereotypy of desmosomal connections suggests development through a precisely specified connectivity code between cell types, with some connections having clear functional relevance (muscle-to-chitin attachments) while others (connections to ciliary cells) may represent unexplored mechanistic interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C152 make inferences about developmental mechanisms (C150) and functional significance (C151-C152). While the stereotypy observation supports the developmental inference, this remains speculative without experimental validation. The speculation about ciliary cell connections (C152) is appropriately tentative but lacks supporting evidence.

results.result: The combined desmosomal and synaptic connectomes provide a foundation for understanding locomotor control in Platynereis, demonstrating that accurate modeling of locomotion requires mapping both synaptic and adhesive networks, with Platynereis being a promising system for in-depth analysis.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C153-C158 summarize the significance and future potential of the work. The claim that both connectomes are needed for understanding locomotion (C158) is well-supported by the data showing how desmosomal connectivity determines tissue influence of motoneurons. The characterization of Platynereis as a promising system (C157) is reasonable given the available tools and data.
